nameStory: This tiny sea slug gets its scientific name from its incredibly specific lifestyle - it lives exclusively on sea squirts (called ascidians by scientists). The species name 'ascidicola' literally means 'ascidian dweller,' making this one of the most accurately named creatures in the ocean!
description: Okenia ascidicola is a microscopic sea slug, one of the nudibranch family, that you'd need a magnifying glass to truly appreciate. These translucent creatures are barely larger than a pinhead, typically reaching only 3-5 millimeters in length. They have a soft, elongated body with finger-like projections called cerata extending from their back, giving them an almost alien appearance. Despite their tiny size, they're specialized predators with a remarkable ability to perfectly match their sea squirt hosts.

idTips.label: Size and habitat
idTips.description: Extremely small (3-5mm) and always found crawling on or near colonial sea squirts, often perfectly camouflaged against their host

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Elongated, soft body with numerous finger-like projections (cerata) extending from the back and sides

idTips.label: Color and transparency
idTips.description: Translucent to semi-transparent body that often takes on the coloration of its sea squirt host

idTips.label: Head region
idTips.description: Two small, club-shaped tentacles (rhinophores) on the head that can be retracted when disturbed

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides very slowly across surfaces with a smooth, flowing motion typical of sea slugs

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters of New England, typically on rocky substrates, pier pilings, and floating docks where colonial sea squirts grow. Look for them in tide pools during low tide or while snorkeling in harbors and protected bays. They're most commonly found between the low tide line and depths of about 30 feet.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing as water temperatures rise and sea squirt colonies start their spring growth. Best spotted during calm, low tide conditions.
seasonality.summer: Most active and numerous during peak warm months when sea squirt colonies are fully developed. Easiest time for observation.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less active as water temperatures cool. May be found deeper as surface waters become less hospitable.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive in New England's cold waters, though some may persist in deeper, more stable temperatures.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your fingernail, Okenia ascidicola is such a specialized hunter that it can steal and incorporate the defensive chemicals from its sea squirt prey, essentially becoming toxic by eating toxic food - nature's ultimate 'you are what you eat' example!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other tiny marine organisms or dismissed as debris on sea squirts. The key difference is their deliberate, gliding movement - unlike hydroids or other sessile creatures that might look similar, these sea slugs will actually crawl around their host.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the most specialized predator-prey relationships in New England waters. The rarity of sightings (only 3 recorded observations) likely reflects both their microscopic size and the specialized knowledge needed to identify them rather than actual scarcity.
compareHints: As the only Okenia species documented in New England waters, it's most similar to other small nudibranchs in the region. However, its exclusive association with sea squirts and extremely small size distinguish it from related species like Coryphella or Eubranchus nudibranchs, which are typically larger and found on different hosts like hydroids.
